items.content:
The NIST Elliptic Curves Seeds Bounty Has Been Claimed

We now know how the seeds of the NIST elliptic curves were generated: they’re not the hash of some saucy sentence, but the output of drand48 seeded with the time, which was indeed in 1997–98.

John Wood, Henry de Valence, Ava Howell, Zack Voase, Lucy Sweet, Amir Omidi, Paul Crowley, Iain McGinniss, Nicholas Carlini, and Steve Weis from Anthropic solved the riddle and on October 15th, 2026, at 01:07:51 UTC, claimed the full bounty I announced three years ago . They chose to donate the prize to ISRG , the non-profit that operates Let’s Encrypt, tripling its value to $36,864 (36 Ki$). Thank you to Amir Omidi, Chris Palmer, Colm MacCárthaigh, David Adrian, David Anderson, Jeff Hodges, Matt Green, Matthew McPherrin, Paul Kehrer, Ryan Sleevi, and Soatok for contributing to the bounty.

This helps fill out a page of cryptographic history, and reinforces our confidence in these critical cryptographic primitives.

The NIST elliptic curves (P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521) were published by NIST in FIPS 186-2 in 2000. They were generated at random according to ANSI X9.62 by taking an arbitrary seed, hashing it with SHA-1, and using the output to derive some of the parameters. Until this week, we had no idea how those arbitrary seeds were picked.

The lore was that Dr. Jerry Solinas, who passed away in early 2023, generated them in 1997 by hashing some English sentences that he later forgot. You can read more in this article by Steve Weis or in the original bounty announcement .

Turns out memory can play tricks on everyone: we now know they were instead generated with the POSIX-standard drand48 random number generator.

The algorithm is as simple as passing the then-current UNIX timestamp to srand48() and then producing one byte at a time with drand48. Each sequence of 20 bytes is tried as a seed following ANSI X9.62 and rejected if the resulting curve is not valid. Some timestamps are used to generate multiple curves, by continuing to try seeds after accepting the first one. I reimplemented the algorithm in Go to verify the claim. Read more in Anthropic’s writeup .

There are two additional undocumented criteria beyond the ANSI X9.62 ones, one fairly clear and one that still escapes us.

If the bit length of the order n of the resulting curve is more than the bit length of the base field p of the curve, the seed is rejected. (The condition is not the stricter n < p , because prime239v2 has p < n < 2²³⁹.)

This leaves us with roughly twice as many valid seeds as were published. We explored a number of explanations for this last bit, and found no good fit. Maybe the same RNG was used to validate seeds, consuming RNG output and skipping some potential candidates, although the “gaps” are not regular. Maybe there was just a bug in one of the algorithms that returned the wrong result half the time; these calculations, which we can now do with off-the-shelf software in minutes, were still very much state-of-the-art in 1997.

MapQuest will now show you where Flock cameras are in your neighborhood
items.content:
MapQuest will now show you where Flock cameras are in your neighborhood

You can see the locations of known outdoor surveillance cameras in the app.

MapQuest has been on quite the unexpected tear over the last couple of months. The mapping service's app surged in popularity after it refused to refer to Lake Ontario as Lake America (unlike Google Maps and Apple Maps ). MapQuest also added useful, long-overdue features like Android Auto support and public transit directions .

The app now has another handy tool . You can toggle a layer that shows known outdoor surveillance cameras and license plate readers.

The layer will show you where  Flock cameras  are. It also displays the locations of cameras from the likes of Motorola Solutions (Vigilant), Genetec, Axis Communications, Axon, Leonardo (ELSAG), Neology, Rekor, PlateSmart, Ubicquia and Verkada. The layer sits alongside options to view traffic and incidents, so it should be easy to find in the app.

MapQuest announced the update with a short video that's set to Rockwell's "Somebody's Watching Me." Chef's kiss, no notes.

You might not be able to easily avoid these cameras on your commute or other usual routes, but the layer may be helpful in illustrating how pervasive these things are in your area. It's useful information to have for those who are trying to rid their neighborhoods of surveillance cams.

items.title: Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins
items.content:
“It’s just timestamps”: the decades-old mystery of the origins of one of the most popular cryptographic standards has been explained.

We pursued this long-standing open question of the cryptographic community to settle concerns about ECDSA, which is one of our most widely used cryptographic standards.

Readers should take this as a fun closing chapter and the end of years of speculation. There is no action to be taken or things to do differently. Most researchers trusted the curves already. Enjoy.

ECDSA is the most widely used elliptic curve cryptography standard. It was adopted by NIST in 2000 as part of the FIPS 186-2 Digital Signature Standard which lists a set of standard elliptic curves of varying sizes and security levels. For curves over prime and binary fields, the specifications published a “seed” parameter whose hash value is used to define the coefficient b of the curve. The provenance of these seeds has been a long-standing question, as they were provided by the NSA with no explanation or justification. As an example, the NIST P-256 curve seed was SEED = C49D3608 86E70493 6A6678E1 139D26B7 819F7E90 with no information where it came from.

Neal Koblitz and Alfred Menezes wrote an excellent summary on this controversy, “ A Riddle Wrapped in an Enigma ”, which discusses the history and concerns around the seed values. This mystery led to an amateur investigation into the origin of the seeds and a bounty for anyone who could find them .

The best story was that Jerry Solinas, longtime NSA employee, generated the seeds using a hash of a humorous passphrase:

“I believe there was a counter rather than multiple hashing, but I don’t know details. The message was along the lines of ‘Give Bob and Jerry a raise’ or ‘Bob and Jerry rule’ or something like that. It was Bob Reiter who actually wrote the code, and he doesn’t remember the details either. Nor were we able to find archives from so long ago. If they exist, they are no doubt sitting on a hard drive near the Ark of the Covenant.”

Unfortunately, Jerry died in 2023 and other colleagues at the time were not responsive, leaving open the question of how these seeds were originally derived.

Several Anthropic employees had unsuccessfully chased the seeds following the tip about it being a hash of a humorous phrase. That turned out to be wrong. In October 2026, a curious Anthropic employee asked an internal research model if it could figure out how those seeds were generated without pointing at the clue.

In under half an hour , Claude discovered the origins of the NIST P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384 and P-521 seeds. None of them were the results of any hash algorithm at all, but rather the output of the C library’s lrand48 random-number generator, seeded with a Unix timestamp!

The algorithm used would sample bytes from the random number generator (RNG) initialized by a Unix timestamp ( t ) for some number of iterations ( n ). Each iteration would draw 20 bytes as a candidate seed. So, the first 20 bytes are candidate 1, the next 20 bytes are candidate 2, and so on. For example, P-256 required 1842 iterations to output the standardized seed.

This is not a cryptographic break, new attack, or weakness in the ECDSA curves. In fact, this makes us more confident the curves were chosen without any backdoors or intentional weaknesses. For many years, people have been suspicious of the origins of the NIST curve parameters. They were presented to NIST without any mention of how they were chosen, leaving people wondering if they may have been chosen to have deliberate backdoors in them. These findings make that much less plausible. The seeds were generated in a very simple way: a common pseudorandom number generator initialized from the clock, which anyone can now reproduce. That leaves much less room for subversion and that we can be confident the parameters are secure.

items.title: The road to iroh 1.0
items.summary: networking
items.content:
It is done. After four years of work and various pivots we have released iroh 1.0.

We have an expanding web site describing how iroh works under the hood, but we think it is important to also understand why we made the decisions that led to the current iroh. So here is a trip down memory lane / our commit history which highlights major turning points and design decisions.

Perhaps more importantly, this post also covers some things we considered but ended up not doing .

Iroh started as a rust implementation of ipfs . We got pretty far implementing various ipfs protocols and had interop with existing ipfs implementations working. Our goal with iroh was to target lightweight and resource constrained devices such as mobile phones.

One area where we were unhappy with existing protocols was blob transfer. We started a working group within the ipfs community to come up with a new protocol, called the move the bytes working group .

For that working group, we worked on a proposal for new blob transfer protocol. We wrote a small library called krakensync . Krakensync used BLAKE3 exclusively for content addressing because BLAKE3 supports verified incremental streaming of large blobs.

After a few days we had a bare algorithm, and wanted to add networking to it to make the demo feel more real. We had only two days before the next meeting, and adding networking via rust-libp2p seemed impossible (Remember that this was before LLM coding assistants!).

I had a tiny bit of previous experience with QUIC , and remembered from a project of a friend of mine, quinn-noise that quinn is both hackable and has a simple idiomatic rust API. So I tried to add networking via quinn and found it an absolute joy to work with.

In parallel to working on the ipfs compatible iroh, we worked on a side project to implement a single narrow real world use case: transfer of deltachat chat history when provisioning a new device. The technical task was to transfer a single large blob of backup data to a new device. There were hard constraints regarding disk and network usage. And the transfer had to be resumable.

We found that we could not implement this very narrow use case with our ipfs based iroh implementation. Doing so would have had less than optimal network performance, and would have pulled in a very large dependency tree.

So we started writing a lightweight sync library from scratch, using QUIC as the networking layer and BLAKE3 verified streaming for large blob transfer.

Despite our best efforts, our main project was still far away from the theoretical limits. Meanwhile our sync side project showed what is possible. So we made the decision to no longer pursue the goal of staying compatible with existing ipfs implementations.

Instead of multiaddrs , endpoints were identified by an Ed25519 public key.

And instead of multiple transport protocols we had just QUIC.

The new iroh was just QUIC based networking using quinn and blob transfer using BLAKE3 verified streaming. Compared to the previous version, the functionality was anemic. But the single thing it did, it did with close to optimal performance. It was a lightweight enough dependency that deltachat could justify including it into their rust code base . And suddenly we had both networking and sync deployed in a real app used by thousands of people across various platforms (windows, linux, iOS, android). The old code lives on in beetle .

We decided to use just QUIC. But QUIC as specified in RFC 9000 has clear client and server roles, where the server is identified by a certificate chain. At the time we had to add a somewhat Rube Goldberg construction on top to make QUIC work for peer-to-peer connections, a self-signed certificate carrying the real public key in a custom X.509 extension , with a signature binding the two.

Also, rustls is a heavy dependency, and its default crypto provider is a C dependency. So there was a temptation to replace the entire TLS encryption scheme with a protocol…

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: In Europe’s tech capital, Irish labor unions are booming amid AI-driven layoffs
items.content:
DUBLIN — The Irish capital, which doubles as Europe's de facto tech capital, hosted two very different AI summits in the past week.

Most eyes were on the International AI Summit , the signature tech event of Ireland's six-month presidency of the Council of the EU, where top brass from the world's biggest tech firms discussed ways to harness artificial intelligence and minimize safety risks.

But the weekend before, a very different conversation was taking place at the Workers' AI Counter Summit , as Ireland's tech workers demanded a say in how the burgeoning technology reshapes the workplace and society.

Ireland's lucrative tech sector has been rattled by waves of AI-driven layoffs — and the country's fledgling tech union has seen an exponential spike in sign-ups from workers who are worried about their future.

There’s an “awakening” happening right now among workers in Ireland’s tech sector, and a growing “awareness that they’re not bulletproof,” said Sinéad Gibney, a social democrat lawmaker who previously worked for Google.

“I do think what we will see is that parts of roles will be automated, which means that people will be competing more heavily for the same roles," she said. "They won't have the same labor power and therefore we're going to see a drop in quality of work, we're going to see more zero-hour contracts, in more places than we already see it.”

The labor movement brewing in Ireland, where many of the world's tech giants have their EU bases, is part of a wider trend among tech workers globally, who have seen their work disrupted by rapidly evolving AI.

Ireland’s dedicated union for tech workers, the Digital and Techworker Alliance (DATA), has seen a five-fold increase in membership since it was first founded in 2023.

In its first year and a half of existence, membership hovered around 270 people. In the past year-and-a-half, it's jumped to more than 1,350 members, DATA organizer John Bohan told POLITICO.  He added that this number tends to spike around layoffs and other actions.

“The tech industry was founded on the idea that it would never have a union, because they're making people rich, and treat them really well,” Bohan said.  “But post-Covid, workforce adjustments happened again and again, with layoffs and declining conditions in the sector. We started to see more people wanting to get organized around redundancies.”

The spike in sign-ups coincides with a wave of layoffs in Ireland’s tech bubble (and the tech sector globally ), as companies corrected pandemic-era overhiring, and diverted investment to AI.

Ireland hosts the EU headquarters of most of the world’s largest tech companies, and more than 170,000 people are employed in the tech sector, according to the country's statistics institute.

Social media giant Meta has roughly halved its workforce in Ireland since the pandemic, axing well over 1,000 roles to offset AI investment and boost efficiency. Separately, Meta subcontractor Covalen also announced massive layoffs earlier this year, cutting more than 700 people.

Video-sharing platform TikTok announced this year it would shed around 300 Irish jobs , mostly from its trust and safety team, shifting the work to other countries, outsourced vendors or automated AI solutions.

A report by the IMF earlier this year warned that Ireland’s labor market is “relatively more exposed” to AI than many advanced economies, partly due to its concentration of tech workers.

The AI race is also creating new jobs on the Irish market – as AI firms like Anthropic and OpenAI are setting up Irish bases and trying to lure Big Tech workers with even bigger salaries.

Amid the uncertainty and volatility of the AI boom, tech workers are turning to unions for the first time as a safety net. One tech worker who used to work in trust and safety at a big tech firm told POLITICO that there used to be a feeling that as a “pampered” tech worker you “can't ask for your rights, because you already have it so much…

Learned Index Lab: Piecewise Geometric Model (PGM-Index) in Rust

A zero-dependency, production-grade implementation of Piecewise Geometric Model (PGM) Learned Index Structures in pure Rust.

This repository demonstrates the paradigm shift away from traditional comparison-based pointer hierarchies (such as B-Trees and LSM block indexes) to mathematical function approximations of Empirical Cumulative Distribution Functions (CDFs) with provable $\epsilon$ error bounds.

Optimal Streaming Piecewise Linear Approximation (PLA)

Statistical Benchmark Suite (10-Run Rigorous Analysis)

3. Clustered Heavy-Tailed Lognormal Distribution

For more than 50 years, database indexing has relied on tree-based data structures ( B-Tree , B+Tree , LSM-Tree ). While mature, B-Trees possess inherent physical constraints on modern CPU architectures:

Pointer Chasing : Navigating down a tree requires sequential memory dereferences across disparate memory addresses, causing recurring L1/L2/L3 cache misses.

High Memory Overhead : Tree nodes require significant metadata per key (child pointers, balance factors, keys, values), consuming 30–50 bytes per entry.

Branch Misprediction : Binary comparisons at each node introduce branch penalties on deeply pipelined modern CPUs.

Learned Indexes (originally introduced by Kraska et al., MIT / Google) reframe indexing as a regression problem:

Given a sorted sequence of keys $K = (k_0, k_1, \dots, k_{N-1})$ , the position of any key $k$ in memory corresponds to the scaled Empirical Cumulative Distribution Function:

$$\text{Pos}(k) \approx N \times \text{CDF}(k)$$

Rather than allocating deep node hierarchies, a PGM-Index partitions the data into a minimal set of linear segments $y = ax + b$ , guaranteeing that the true position of any indexed key is within a strict error window $[y - \epsilon, y + \epsilon]$ .

Optimal Streaming Piecewise Linear Approximation (PLA)

The index builder executes in a single streaming pass ( $O(N)$ time, $O(1)$ extra space).

For a segment starting at point $(x_0, y_0)$ and a given maximum error tolerance $\epsilon$ :

Each subsequent point $(x_i, y_i)$ restricts the feasible slope interval $[s_{\min}, s_{\max}]$ :

$$s_{\min} = \max_{j} \left[ \frac{(y_j - \epsilon) - y_0}{x_j - x_0} \right]$$

$$s_{\max} = \min_{j} \left[ \frac{(y_j + \epsilon) - y_0}{x_j - x_0} \right]$$

As long as $s_{\min} \le s_{\max}$ , all points observed so far can be represented by a single straight line with error at most $\epsilon$ . Once $s_{\min} > s_{\max}$ , the segment is finalized with slope $s = \frac{s_{\min} + s_{\max}}{2}$ , and a new segment starts.

The responsible segment is found via a rapid binary search across the segment array ( $O(\log S)$ where $S \ll N$ ).

The position estimate is computed directly via ALU instructions:

$$\text{Pos}_{\text{approx}} = \text{round}(y_0 + s \cdot (k - x_0))$$

The exact match is retrieved via a local binary search bounded strictly inside:

$$[\max(0, \text{Pos} {\text{approx}} - \epsilon), \min(N - 1, \text{Pos} {\text{approx}} + \epsilon)]$$

Time Complexity : $O(\log S + \log \epsilon)$

Space Complexity : $O(S)$ where $S \approx \frac{N}{\text{compression ratio}}$

Correctness : 100% exact (0 false positives, 0 false negatives).

Contiguous array of $(a, b, k_0)$ segments

1 affine math evaluation + local L1 search

Eliminates unpredictable pointer chasing

All benchmarks were measured locally on x86_64 hardware using Rust 1.99 in --release mode.

Each scenario was executed over 10 consecutive runs with distinct randomized seeds to eliminate CPU scheduling noise and warm-cache anomalies.

items.title: 90% of US working hours are spent on tasks not covered well by AI benchmarks
items.content:
AI benchmarks have multiplied in recent years, but coverage of economically valuable work remains limited. To measure this, we compiled relevant benchmarks to measure their coverage of American jobs. This Benchmark Map is our first step toward building a comprehensive, continuously updated resource for understanding AI capabilities across the economy.

Each tile represents one of the 923 O*NET occupations making up the US labor force, grouped into 22 job families. Occupations are shaded according to the share of their tasks which are represented in our initial list of AI benchmarks. A single benchmark prompt can be mapped to multiple O*NET tasks.

In our data set: only 208 of 923 occupations have a task with at least 5 benchmark prompts , and 6 of 22 job families have no such occupations.

Our findings suggest that 90% of American working hours are spent on tasks with little or no coverage from existing benchmarks . This makes it very hard to know how good AI models are at the work Americans actually do.

The coverage of existing benchmarks is not random, either. Our map suggests that the AI community is focusing on the largest labor markets first:

Annualized occupation wage bill (log scale)

Each point shows the estimated probability that an O*NET task with a given AI-exposure tag belonging to an occupation with a given wage-bill will be covered by at least 5 prompts in our benchmark index. AI-exposure tags are binary and come from Eloundou et al. (2023) . Occupation wage-bills are calculated from BLS estimates of the mean wage and number of Americans working in each occupation, assuming a 40 hour work week. Estimated coverage probabilities come from a task-level logistic regression of coverage probability on AI-exposure and log occupational wage bill. Error bars are pointwise 95% delta-method confidence intervals based on standard errors clustered at the occupation group level.

For example, benchmarks in our initial list heavily cover AI-exposed lawyers’ tasks, but barely cover any of the O*NET tasks of similarly AI-exposed legal secretaries or court clerks. The long tail of smaller, middle-income knowledge work jobs appears undercovered.

As we build out our coverage of model capabilities across the economy, we hope to both surface and help fill more gaps in our understanding of what models can do.

To break down the economy into sectors, occupations, and tasks, we used the US Department of Labor’s O*NET taxonomy. O*NET divides the US workforce into 923 occupations; for each occupation, O*NET attempts to provide a comprehensive list of “tasks” which make up the occupation, totaling 18,797 tasks across all occupations.

To measure benchmark coverage, we start with a list of 29 benchmarks selected for their quality and economic relevance. (The full list and selection criteria are in the Benchmark Index tab). In selecting benchmarks for this list, we prioritized:

Following work by Wang et al. , we then ask an LLM judge to tag each benchmark prompt with as many O*NET tasks as it thinks correspond to that prompt. We validate our LLM tagging with human expert tags on Mercor’s APEX benchmarks, a subset of this list of 29. On the Benchmark Map, an O*NET task counts as “covered” if our LLM judge has mapped it to at least 5 prompts from our 29 benchmarks.

To estimate the total share of working hours Americans spend on tasks covered by benchmarks on this list, we combine our coverage estimates with Hatgis-Kessell et al. ’s LLM-derived estimates of the working time share of each O*NET task.

A more detailed account of our methodology can be found in the Methodology tab.

Our estimates of total economic coverage, and of patterns in coverage, all come from the initial list of 29 benchmarks we chose. Updates on my research and expository papers, discussion of open problems, and other maths-related topics. By Terence Tao

15 October, 2026 in guest blog , opinion | Tags: Rikab Gambhir | by Terence Tao

[This is a guest post by Rikab Gambhir . This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.]

and I did not speak out, because I was not an artist.

and I did not speak out, because I was not a mathematician.

and it was actually really cool and they gave me free tokens and promised to solve my entire field for me and now I can finally devote myself to the important work of publishing papers instead of doing physics

In early October, OpenAI fulfilled every mathematician’s childhood dream.

I am not a mathematician myself (merely a theoretical particle physicist, which some argue barely counts as a scientist either), so I can’t 100% say for certain what inspires someone to pursue mathematics. But, I imagine this dream is common to all academics:

Looking up at the stars in wonderment, or enjoying a complex puzzle game, or being inspired by an encouraging teacher, and dreaming that one day an unfeeling corporate robot[1] will burn a rainforest to compile a list of 700 highly obscure barely-readable facts that *might* be true that nobody can understand as part of a marketing gimmick to raise hype for an IPO[2] .

This is probably why most of you reading this got into academia. At least, that’s why I did.

In 1941, Jorge Luis Borges imagined a library containing every possible book that could ever be written. Somewhere in this Library of Babel is a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, the complete all-orders theory of quantum gravity, and all the papers I will ever write. Of course, there are also incorrect proofs, theories, and misleading Lean certificates , but that is besides the point.

By the research standards of 2026, Borges’s Library of Babel would be the most successful research institution in human history, containing an inconceivably large number of potentially correct mathematical and physical results, blowing OpenAI’s mere 722 write-ups and even the physics community’s recent 2500 write-ups out of the water.

Of course, most recognize that Borges was a visionless fool who failed to recognize the commercial potential of his library, as he never actually built it. He did not have the entrepreneurial STEM-spirit to raise venture capital, launch an IPO, and announce that he had the potential to solve all of mathematics. He was too concerned about the futility of sorting through randomized slop trying to understand what is correct and what isn’t and how to understand it all. But what did Borges know? He was only a writer, and we have already established that artists are obsolete.

Fortunately, OpenAI has brought us one step closer to realizing Borges’s vision. Rather than generating every possible mathematical paper, they’ve found a way to probabilistically generate things that look correct. An important aspect of this increase in efficiency is outsourcing the tedious, unprestigious, and unprofitable work of determining the actual correctness and understanding to the mathematics community (in the past, this was reserved typically for the group writing the paper), while also not wasting any time making the papers human-comprehensible. This is, of course, a tremendous breakthrough. In centuries past, scientists and mathematicians were limited in their ability to solve problems by their ability to understand the solutions. This bottleneck has been removed, and now there is no theoretical limit to the amount of scientific and mathematical factoids we can fail to understand.

From what I know about the academic community (mostly from Twitter and LinkedIn, which I assume are representative), there seems to be near-unanimous agreement that the purpose of math and science research is to gather a large quantity of potentially true factoids in a repository that nobody will actually ever read,…

items.title: I Love Software Rendering
items.content:
I love software rendering. The best DOS experience I’ve had in a long while was Quake in its software renderer at 800×600, running at a locked 60fps on my Dell OptiPlex 380 . It’s one of the best-looking things I’ve seen a DOS game do.

That’s not how most people remember those games looking. In the 90s you either ran them in software at a low resolution, or you bought a 3D card and played the accelerated version. Today there’s a third option: run the software renderer on a machine fast enough to push it at resolutions nobody could use back then.

In a software-rendered game, the CPU draws every pixel. There’s no 3D card involved: the game works out each frame in its own code and writes it straight to video memory. Doom, Duke Nukem 3D, Blood and the original Quake all work this way.

When 3D cards arrived, many games got accelerated versions. GLQuake came after Quake, and Blood and Tomb Raider got 3dfx modes. Those versions hand the drawing to the graphics card, and they look different.

It’s sharp. Software renderers generally sample textures pixel by pixel, so every texel stays a crisp square. Early 3D cards smoothed textures with bilinear filtering, which looked impressive in 1997 but turns everything soft and blurry to my eye now.

It’s gritty. Most of these games ran in 256 colours, with lighting done through lookup tables into that palette. Shadows fall off in visible steps rather than smooth gradients. Technically that’s colour banding, a limitation. In practice it gives the games a rough, grimy texture that I really like, and that hardware rendering smooths away.

It’s how the games were built. Quake was released with its software renderer, and GLQuake followed. Doom and the Build engine games were designed around their software renderers from the start.

It isn’t always the better option. When I got a Voodoo 2 running in a modern PC , Blood ran fast in its 3dfx mode, but the VESA software modes were the better-looking option. Tomb Raider went the other way: its underwater sections look noticeably better accelerated than in the DOS software renderer. So it’s a preference, not a rule. But for most of the games I care about, I’d pick the software renderer.

It’s not just nostalgia, either. Ion Fury, a Build engine game from 2019, still ships with a software renderer.

Software rendering scales with the CPU. Every extra pixel is work for the processor, so the high VESA resolutions that many late DOS games offered were well beyond the hardware of the day.

Modern hardware can power through most of it. On the OptiPlex 380, Quake at 800×600 holds a locked 60fps. But the heaviest games still push even very fast machines. In his video on the Portwell RUBY-9719 , Rasteri shows Build engine games needing far more power at high resolutions, to the point where even a 3.3GHz quad-core Xeon “isn’t quite enough to run Shadow Warrior at full 1600 by 1200”.

So if you want to see these games at their best, you want the fastest machine you can get that still runs them.

There are other ways to get software rendering on a modern PC. Source ports of Doom and Quake run software renderers on Windows, and Ion Fury runs on Windows natively. They’re great.

What I’m after is the original DOS versions running as they were released, on real hardware. DOSBox is the obvious alternative, but some DOS titles struggle in DOSBox, while on real hardware they behave exactly as intended.

That leaves one more problem: sound. A fast machine running native DOS needs a sound card the games can talk to, and modern PCs don’t have one. That’s a story of its own.

You are seeing this because the administrator of this website has set up Anubis to protect the server against the scourge of AI companies aggressively scraping websites. This can and does cause downtime for the websites, which makes their resources inaccessible for everyone.

Anubis is a compromise. Anubis uses a Proof-of-Work scheme in the vein of Hashcash, a proposed proof-of-work scheme for reducing email spam. The idea is that at individual scales the additional load is ignorable, but at mass scraper levels it adds up and makes scraping much more expensive.

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: Motivated Reasoning and Confirmation Bias Drive Viral Claims of “Russian Bot” Declines
items.content:
Over the last 72 hours, the Internet has been overwhelmed with reports of something miraculous: that “Russian social media activity” had dropped dramatically following Ukrainian drone strikes on Yandex data centers.

It is true that Ukrainian drones knocked out three of Yandex’s data centers , in a solid blow to Russia’s economy and information processing capacity — at Sasovo on October 8, Kaluga on October 9 and Vladimir on October 11.

But then people started sharing charts that alleged that Russian “bot traffic” had collapsed to almost nothing. The trolls on social media, they claimed, had finally been unplugged.

It was a great story. The only problem? It isn’t true — or at least there is no quantifiable evidence (yet) that supports the claim. As we did last week following reports of plague in Irkutsk (remember that?), we built a live tracker to sort out facts from fiction. And we’ve made every effort to test the claims beyond the vibes. Those efforts have, so far, failed to produce any claims or data that support the “Russian Bot Miracle of 2026.” Here’s what we did find.

The Russian Bot Collapse Report: did Russia’s bots really go quiet?

A sourced, live check on the viral claim that Ukraine’s strikes on Yandex data centers silenced Russian social-media bots: what the data measures, what it doesn’t, and who is spreading which claims.

The viral chart came from Cloudflare Radar , and the numbers were real. But Cloudflare’s “bot” category counts automated web requests coming from Yandex’s own network, and almost all of that is YandexBot, the crawler Yandex uses to index the web for its search engine. When the data centers went dark, the crawler stopped crawling. Cloudflare itself told BBC Verify the drop was “not necessarily bot behaviour on social media platforms.”

Cloudflare Radar’s chart of web requests from Yandex’s network, October 5–12. The drop reflects Yandex’s search crawler going offline, not social-media bots ( Cloudflare Radar ). Tom’s Hardware ran the numbers under a headline saying Yandex’s bot traffic had been “nearly eliminated overnight” and told readers “the world is getting a break from Russian bots.” However, this was simply a misreading of the data, probably made in error, but by a publication that should know better.

Partly, there is a language problem: the word “bot” is overloaded. What people talk about when they are talking about coordinated inauthentic social media activity is probably better described by the word “troll.” Bots (automated programs, such as the crawlers that index the web for search engines) are a legitimate part of web infrastructure, and are a necessary part of search engine technology.

What the Russian troll networks actually show

Researchers who actually count Russian influence accounts (including America 2.0 ) saw no such thing. Res Futura , which follows about 500 pro-Russian accounts on Polish X, found normal activity through the strikes, and on October 13 the accounts’ hourly activity was up 45% on the day before.

The think tank Polisphere , watching nearly 10,000 accounts in German-speaking countries, found no statistically noticeable decline. Poland’s NASK found none either. Researchers at dTeam told BBC Verify they had seen no “traffic change from known Russian accounts and bot clusters on any platform,” and that the Storm-1516 and Matryoshka operations were still active.

There was one real signal, however. The automated “ Pravda ” news network, which floods the web with pro-Kremlin articles, lost about half its output for roughly 13 hours after the Vladimir strike, then recovered. This suggests it used a pipeline that leaned on something at Yandex, and quickly routed around it. Our tracker breaks all of this out network by network .

This story (data centers hit; bots gone) was flawed from the start, and it was easy to see; the graphs shared (which also included a fake graph showing a drop in AfD traffic) were obviously misconstrued and were immediately debunked…

items.title: Quantum bioinformatics reality check: most studies never touch real quantum
items.content:
Quantum bioinformatics reality check: most studies never touch real quantum hardware

Quantum computing has been pitched as the future engine of computational biology, promising to crack problems that would take classical supercomputers centuries to solve. But a sweeping new systematic review suggests the field is far closer to its proof-of-concept childhood than its headline writers would have you believe. Researchers at Sapienza University of Rome and the University of Tuscia analyzed fifty-three experimental studies spanning genome assembly, protein folding, phylogenetics, and biomedical machine learning, and their verdict is stark: while quantum bioinformatics has produced viable prototypes, the vast majority of published results never touch real quantum hardware, and fewer than a third can be independently verified at all.

The review, published in Frontiers in High Performance Computing, was designed to separate theoretical promise from empirical reality. The authors systematically assessed experimental studies across four core biological domains, evaluating each one by its underlying computational paradigm, the scale of its datasets, the quality of its comparisons against classical baselines, and its adherence to open-science reproducibility standards. The findings reveal a field dominated by classical simulations and quantum-inspired heuristics rather than genuine quantum execution, with nearly 77 percent of implementations restricted to heavily reduced toy datasets due to current technological constraints.

The technical landscape of quantum bioinformatics is more fragmented than the term quantum computing suggests. The review distinguishes four paradigms: quantum annealing, gate-based quantum computing, quantum-inspired algorithms, and classical simulation. Quantum annealing, most commonly executed on D-Wave processors, encodes biological problems as Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) problems or Ising models, where the solution corresponds to the minimum-energy configuration of a physical system. Gate-based quantum computing, by contrast, is a more general-purpose and theoretically universal model, manipulating qubits through sequences of quantum gates arranged in circuits. Quantum-inspired methods borrow concepts from quantum mechanics, such as superposition-like probability amplitudes, but execute entirely on classical hardware. Classical simulators, such as Qiskit, reproduce the behavior of quantum circuits without a physical quantum processor.

The distribution of these paradigms across the reviewed literature is telling. Classical simulations of quantum circuits represent the dominant approach, accounting for 47 percent of the 53 studies. Quantum annealing and quantum-inspired algorithms each account for 21 percent, while gate-based quantum computing, the paradigm most closely associated with universal quantum advantage, accounts for just 11 percent. Among studies utilizing real quantum hardware, D-Wave quantum annealers dominate the landscape, spanning three hardware generations from the D-Wave 2X through the 2000Q to the Advantage. Only six studies employed gate-based quantum processors, distributed across IBM, IonQ, Rigetti, and QuantumCTek systems.

Several factors explain D-Wave’s predominance. Many core bioinformatics problems, from genome assembly to RNA folding, codon optimization, and protein design, can be naturally reformulated as combinatorial optimization problems expressible as QUBO or Ising Hamiltonians, which is precisely the class of problems quantum annealers are purpose-built to solve. D-Wave systems also offer significantly higher qubit counts than current gate-based processors, with the Advantage2 providing over 4,400 qubits compared to the hundreds available on the largest gate-based devices. items.content:
Local and Distributed Large LLM Inference with MLX and RDMA on Mac Studio

MLX on Mac with Apple silicon lets AI researchers and developers experiment locally with the latest models and methods in a private environment. The open-source array framework leverages the unified memory architecture of Apple silicon, enabling anyone to run new inference and fine-tuning methods on their own hardware and explore other AI techniques. In a previous post , we highlighted the advantages of the M5 architecture and its GPU Neural Accelerators.

In this post, we show how to run the latest frontier-class model — Muse Spark Open, with nearly a trillion parameters — right from your desk, using the latest version of MLX, released today. On a cluster of four Mac Studios, Muse Spark Open generates over 36 tokens per second (see Figure 1 ), well above average human reading speed.

Beginning on a single Mac Studio (up to 512GB of unified memory), then scaling out across multiple Macs with the RDMA over Thunderbolt driver, below we share an overview of the range of models you can now run on Mac Studio.

We benchmark several popular open-weight LLMs on Mac Studio , using the MLX LM package, as described in our prior post . We compare two generations of Mac Studio: the recently released M5 Ultra and the previous generation, M3 Ultra. The M5 generation features the GPU Neural Accelerator, which supports dedicated matrix multiplication operations, essential for many machine learning workloads.

We evaluate three frontier-class models ( Table 1 ) spanning a wide range of sizes (in billions of parameters, B): the newly released Muse Spark Open (816 B), Mistral Medium 3.5 (128 B), and Qwen 3.8 (27 B). Muse Spark Open is a mixture of experts (MoE) model, which keeps only a fraction of its experts — and thus parameters — active, reducing compute at inference, and it is evaluated in NVFP4 precision. Mistral Medium 3.5 and Qwen 3.8 are dense architectures, where all parameters are active at inference, and they are evaluated in their native floating-point precision (FP8 and BF16, respectively).

Our evaluation measures three metrics across a range of context sizes: time to first token (TTFT, in seconds), generation throughput (in tokens/second), and peak power usage (in watts). All the performance numbers in this post were obtained with mlx_lm.benchmark . A popular use of local LLMs on Mac Studio is running agentic experiences in a private environment, including agentic coding applications that often need large contexts. We therefore report performance at both 8,192 and 65,536 context sizes.

Raw TTFT and decode throughput are reported in Table 2 and Table 3 , respectively.

Qwen 3.8 27B and Mistral Medium 3.5 128B fit comfortably on a single Mac Studio with 512GB, taking up to 68GB and 158GB of RAM in the large context size (65,536 tokens) setup. items.title: The Decoherence Trap: When AI slop drowns out the signal in an endless sea of noise
items.summary: vibecoding
items.content:
This essay introduces the concept of decoherence : the accumulation of locally valid but mutually incompatible or redundant models within a system, such that the cost of change is dominated by translating among those models and preventing unintended side-effects.

Step 600 Step 200 Start Step 200 Step 600

In other words, it's what happens when slop drowns out the signal in an endless sea of noise.

Decoherence grows relative to the rate of change of a system, and it increases faster the more decoherent a system is, resulting in runaway exponential growth. It is not a new phenomenon, and humans have always countered it through carefully finding ways to do more with less, unifying disparate patterns and models into a cohesive whole. However, the widespread use of AI is currently producing it at a rate that is unsustainable.

The good news is that this rules out the specter of runaway recursive self-improvement, the intelligence explosion that goes parabolic before anyone can react, as decoherence both prevents AI from improving in a bubble and limits the rate at which it can improve outside of it. The bad news is that we are barreling toward a different kind of disaster: Decoherence Collapse.

Imagine a building, let's say a small office tower. When this building was built, they used a type of pipe that will degrade over time and eventually need to be replaced. This is standard infrastructural debt ; basic wear and tear, as they say.

Then, let's say that when it comes time to replace the pipes, you need to change them over to a new standard. This could be because of new building code requirements, because the old pipes simply aren't made anymore, or because the new pipes are much better and easier to maintain. This is standard technical advancement debt , the need to upgrade and transition due to the forward progress of technology over time.

There is a third form of debt that can arise based on how the transition from old pipes to new pipes is done. Consider the following options:

Shut down the building and replace all of the pipes at once. This is a very disruptive and expensive method, since you can't use the building while the process is underway and you have to pay for the replacement up front. But the process is complete by the end of it.

Shut down each floor, one at a time, and replace the pipes on that floor. This is less disruptive overall, but somewhat more expensive because you still have to pay up front, and you have to pay a premium for the extra labor required to keep things running smoothly as the work goes on.

Replace the pipes as needed, when they begin to fail. This is the least disruptive strategy, and it allows you to amortize the cost of replacing all of the pipes over time, with one small repair after another.

For most people, option 3 is very appealing. It allows them to keep things running smoothly and to spread out the cost of maintenance. And if we can just make like the Ship of Theseus [ 1 ] and replace the pipes one at a time, why shouldn't we?

Well, for one thing, it creates decoherence .

And decoherence is, by far, the worst form of tech debt.

The Ship of Theseus actually gives us a good lens for understanding the true scope of decoherence. We know how to build ships made of wood, and we know how to build ships made of steel. You can repair a ship one piece at a time with the same material, as the original thought experiment goes, and the ship remains functional, with all of the original designs and structures that went into it intact.

But do we know how to build every iteration of a ship in between wood and steel? Could you, say, slowly replace every piece of a man-of-war and incrementally turn it into a modern destroyer? And have it functional (for some definition of functional) at every step in the process?

It's not that the answer is an absolute "no". If we are creative enough, if we had the best minds working on it, then I'm sure there would be some path to doing this. But it would…

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. When the input to parse ends in a separator and a lone CR, the parser treats the end of the input as the next character and stores the end-of-file marker in the field as the byte 0xFF. With binary set, parse("a,\r") returns the fields "a" and "\xFF". On UTF-8 flagged input the last field is a UTF-8 flagged string holding that lone byte, which is malformed UTF-8. The same input with a non-empty last field is rejected as an error. items.title: Waymo in Toronto
items.content:
Waymo is officially heading to Canada! We’re laying the groundwork for our fully autonomous ride-hailing service in Toronto, investing in local facilities and jobs, with the goal of welcoming our first riders in 2028.

In the coming days, you’ll start to see Waymo vehicles on the streets of Toronto as we begin driving manually. We are taking a rigorous, phased, safety-first approach starting with high-definition mapping of local street networks and testing with trained autonomous specialists behind the wheel. This validation period will ensure the Waymo Driver adapts seamlessly to Toronto’s distinct driving conditions.

“Expanding into Canada marks an important milestone in Waymo’s global journey,” said Waymo co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana. “Toronto is one of the world’s great cities — innovative, diverse, and forward-looking. We’re proud to bring the Waymo Driver to Canada’s largest city and to partner with the vibrant business, arts and cultural communities that share our commitment to safer streets and more accessible mobility.”

To serve Toronto, we’re partnering with Element Fleet Management, a Toronto-headquartered company and global leader in intelligent fleet and mobility solutions that will provide end-to-end fleet management services. Together with Element and our partners, we’ll invest in hundreds of roles over time spanning fleet maintenance, validation driving, customer service, and other operations functions that support our service. This deep partnership builds on Waymo’s existing ties to Canada, which includes our long-term investor relationship with the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and our manufacturing partner, Magna International.

"As a Canadian company, we are proud to be expanding our partnership with Waymo to help bring autonomous ride-hailing to Toronto,” said Laura Dottori-Attanasio, Chief Executive Officer, Element Fleet Management. Together with Waymo, Element will help create employment opportunities providing the fleet expertise, operational capabilities, and intelligent mobility solutions needed to support autonomous fleets reliably and at scale."

items.content:
If you've spent a considerable amount of time surfing the internet (and especially the Small Web), you might have seen an 88x31 button, or a few dozen of them. Some of them look like this:

However, the nice thing about computer displays is that they are able to cope with quickly changing visuals, hence some have animation:

I have noticed that among very numerous examples , i haven't seen any that'd go very far in that axis. Usually the animations are there just to catch your eye, or to display several words in succession. But why not Moby Dick?

I was surprised to find that there seems to be no limit to the number of frames in a GIF file, and that the maximum resolution is 2^16 by 2^16, which is 4295 megapixels. We are of course limiting ourselves to just 88 by 31 pixels (or 0.003 megapixel), which might mean that regular text fonts don't get much space to shine — Arial, for example, seems to become legible at a minimum of 10 pixels height, which allows us to display about eleven words at once.

As is often the case in computing, popular conventions end up upsetting someone enough that they develop an alternative way. In this case the alternative we're looking for are fonts designed to be legible at extremely low font sizes. There are some as small as 3x3, but personally I find TomThumb to be the golden middle here. You can get TomThumb in truetype here .

Firstly, you will want to obtain a plain text copy of the book's content. The methods might vary depending on what formats you have access to — you can use OCR to grab the text from a physical book , with an .EPUB or .PDF you can convert them (or even copy text manually), or you might get lucky and find what you're looking already shipped as a plain text .txt file, as is the case with Moby Dick .

I downloaded the file and stripped the license at the start and the end. I also cropped off everything before the first chapter.

If we take our button, which is 88x31, and our font, which is 6x4 (5x3 + spacing), we find that we can fit 5 rows of 22 characters each. ImageMagick, the tool we're going to use, is not very good at laying out text, so it'd be wise to take care of that ourselves. There's several ways to do this, but the neatest one uses three posix tools: cat, tr and fold:

cat is used to send the text to tr. tr translates each newline into a space, condensing the whole text file into one line. fold then takes that one line, splits it into multiple lines that are up to 22 characters wide (-w 22), and tries to avoid splitting words in half (-s).

It's likely that at this point, your text looks fine. Mine was a bit garbled up, because fold doesn't handle multibyte characters well. items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: Mull: note-taking with a language server / vscode extension
items.summary: editors
items.content:
Mull is a tool for managing a wiki stored in a plain text file. It has a Visual Studio Code / Cursor extension which provides syntax highlighting, hover previews, completions, diagnostics, formatting, refactoring, etc.

A wiki is a text file with a .mull extension. It contains pages which link to each other, all in the same file. Here's a little wiki with 3 pages:

My go-to breakfast is [ Pancakes ] with fresh [ Lemons ] .

Each page starts with a # Title , followed by the contents of the page. To link to a page, use square brackets like [Lemons] . When you type the opening [ , autocomplete kicks in to help you find the page you're looking for.

Every wiki starts with a Home page. Mull requires that every other page is reachable (directly or indirectly) by following links, starting from Home . This rule promotes a basic form of organization that doesn't involve any hierarchical structure. Pages serve the roles traditionally filled by files and directories.

Mull formats the wiki when you save the file (default), or when you explicitly request it. It chooses the ordering of the pages in the file based on the links between them, so you don't have to think about it. Linking to pages is the only way to organize them.

You can link to files like photos, spreadsheets, or anything else. Mull checks that the linked files actually exist, and you can preview them without leaving the editor.

Files go in a directory next to the wiki named after the wiki, with the .mull extension replaced with _files . For example, if the wiki is my_wiki.mull , the files go in my_wiki_files . If you have a file called my_wiki_files/photos/beach.jpg , you can link it with [/photos/beach.jpg] . You can also link to directories like [/photos/] .

Autocomplete helps you enter the names of files and directories when linking to them. You can also drag-and-drop (while holding the Shift key) or paste files directly into the editor.

Just as every page must be reachable from Home , every file in <wiki>_files (if it exists) must be linked to from the wiki. A link to a directory implicitly counts as linking to everything inside it. An empty directory needs a link of its own.

A portal is a window into another page. It holds a copy of the page's contents, and Mull keeps them in sync. For example, if you have a page called Pancakes , you can open a portal to it from another page like this:

When the wiki is formatted (e.g., on save), that line will be expanded into a copy of the page:

You can edit the page or any of its portals, and formatting will propagate your edits to the rest.

Suppose you have a list that you want to keep sorted:

Mull can help with this; you just have to teach it about sorting. Create a file called <wiki>_files/scripts/sort.sh with the following contents:

Make it executable with chmod +x <wiki>_files/scripts/sort.sh .

Now you can put the list in a sort block:

Mull will then sort the list automatically whenever the wiki is formatted (e.g., on save). That sorting script accepts arguments, so you can, for example, sort in reverse order with ::: sort -r .

Using a script in a block counts as linking to it, so it doesn't need to be linked to from the wiki like other files in <wiki>_files . An unused script still needs a link (e.g., [/scripts/sort.sh] ) somewhere in the wiki.

To use a special symbol like [ or ] literally, put a backslash before it, like \[ . You can also use backticks to denote verbatim text like `this` , as in Markdown. Fenced code blocks are supported too, with syntax highlighting for common languages.

I'm learning Python, currently working on a [ Dice game ] .

No escaping is necessary inside page titles or code.

items.title: Epic says its new vibe-coded Epic Games Launcher is faster than Steam
items.content:
Nearly eight years after Epic took on Steam with its own Game Store and launcher, the Fortnite maker is deploying a new tool to give it an edge over Valve: vibe coding.

In announcing the new publicly available “Preview” build of its Epic Games Launcher, Epic writes that “programming is hard. So, instead of doing that, we vibe coded a new Epic Games Launcher that’s way faster and more responsive than the current one, and has a new look.” And while that might sound a little tongue-in-cheek, Epic Games Store General Manager and VP Martin Keely told PC Gamer that the team “started from scratch” and used AI as “a tool to write and review new features and new capabilities from the ground up in a different tech stack than what we had previously.” The goal, Keely said, was to “look at functionality that existed [in the current Epic Games Launcher] and [say] we want to replicate that, but not the code itself.”

Speaking to IGN , Keely clarified that using AI to code the new Launcher “made us more efficient and allowed a small team to rewrite the code base and be able to launch it faster across platforms, support Windows and Mac, and we’re going to have a Linux version as well.”

We vibe coded the Epic Games Launcher to be faster than the other guy.

Don’t believe us? Test it out for yourself in Preview:

https://t.co/pdtAeEIri4 https://t.co/aMxojUUVPV

— Epic Games Store (@EpicGames) October 14, 2026

The focus on startup speed extends to Epic’s social media announcement , which once again stresses that “we vibe coded the Epic Games Launcher to be faster than the other guy.” Ars’ own testing confirms that the new Launcher goes from a cold start to the store page a few seconds faster than Steam (assuming no login or update issues get in the way). Epic also claims the new Launcher can restore from the system tray to the Library screen slightly faster than Steam, though the claimed difference of 0.06 seconds in this seems so small as to be unnoticeable (and was in our testing).

Epic announced a ground-up “storefront rearchitecture” and “Launcher V2 private Beta” in an Unreal Fest presentation in June . At the time, the company said the new Launcher would have “5x faster cold start” times and help solve challenges that “every developer in this room and every player” has experienced with the current Launcher.

The term “vibe coding” still carries heavy connotations of quickly thrown-together slop that could hide crucial errors beneath the surface. On social media, Epic warns that its Launcher Preview “will have some bugs” that early testers can help squash with a feedback form. The announcement post also warns that the vibe-coded Preview is currently “light on features”— an FAQ clarifies that “certain social features and account management options” haven’t made it over from the legacy version just yet.

That said, the new Preview launcher adds some long-requested features, such as a Recent Games list and a centralized downloads hub for tracking network activity. And Epic writes that it is “working toward feature parity” between the new Launcher and the old one.

Epic’s release of the new “vibe coded” Launcher preview comes just days after a Bloomberg report suggesting the company is pivoting to an “AI first” development model for an upcoming Star Wars and Marvel-themed shooter. “We have a huge pivot underway here at Epic, moving developers around to retool for maximum AI acceleration,” Epic CEO Tim Sweeney wrote on social media on Monday. “The aim isn’t to do the same stuff with fewer people, but to enable everyone here to build MORE and BETTER stuff, and to bring the benefits to all teams using Unreal.”
