items.summary: openbsd, security
items.content:
Big Fish: Exploiting a 37-Year-Old Kernel Bug in OpenBSD

Calif frequently publishes our offensive research and work, but we otherwise don't draw much attention to the defensive work we do — assisting open source projects with remediation, patch generation, cryptographic improvements, and internal engineering projects we carry out for our clients.

Earlier this year, we reported some vulnerabilities, often along with suggested patches to OpenBSD. One traced back roughly 37 years to the original BSD sources , where a shared memory attachment counter was defined as a signed 16-bit short. Repeatedly forking a process with shared memory attachment records could push that counter past its maximum value of 32,767, causing it to wrap to a negative value. This integer overflow could lead to a use-after-free via a race condition; combined with a separate out-of-bounds write in the kernel, it allowed local privilege escalation to root. The issues were addressed in errata 026 and 018 , respectively.

We managed to get local root in OpenBSD with KARL / SMAP / SMEP enabled without the use of an information disclosure vulnerability via the following path:

Map 127 SysV shared memory segments, unmap them via munmap() , and fork 259 processes to wrap the shared memory attach count to -32,643. Perform heap grooming and layout, using metrics from sysctl( KERN_MALLOCSTATS) (such as kb_total and kb_totalfree ) to track allocations and determine when new pages are allocated. Win the race condition using IPC_RMID in one process while attaching a new size-confused shared memory segment in a helper process. Align IP socket allocations and set IP_MULTICAST_TTL to a non-default value of 2 to allocate a persistent 16-byte struct ip_moptions . Its final word packs two 16-bit counters: imo + 12 = imo_num_memberships | imo_max_memberships << 16 . Trigger the conditional -1 out-of-bounds write to overwrite both the number of memberships and maximum memberships fields. close() the socket to traverse the group members, triggering atomic decrements that modify the PTE self-referential mapping twice, switching it from user to supervisor accessible mapping, and achieving kernel code execution by overwriting a predictable kernel pointer. Clean up shared memory accounting and restore the overwritten kernel pointer to obtain a root shell.

That's the short of the matter , the longer version is more interesting , including the history of the vulnerability, as a short shm_nattch can be traced back ~37 years ago , in the original BSD sources.

Taking a step back, this vulnerability ended up getting code execution via a write what where primitive, where the write was caused by a TAILQ_REMOVE , the what was our userland memory mapping that was made supervisor mode accessible to bypass SMAP / SMEP , and the where was a predictable kernel pointer location.

While OpenBSD's KARL relinks the kernel binary to randomize both function and data addresses, the kernel's memory allocators remain deterministic. Both the boot-time allocator and the best-fit allocator lack base address randomization. Consequently, early boot allocations consistently land at predictable locations across boots on the same hardware. When these predictable structure allocations contain function pointers, they become ideal targets for exploitation. For instance, the exploit reliably targets the lo0 and enc0 ioctl handlers, overwriting one to gain control flow and using the other to restore the overwritten pointer.

Aside from the aforementioned errata fixes, there's several other approaches that can be taken to either eliminate or reduce the likelihood of those avenues being used again.

Firstly, we can implement safe-unlinking, a technique that checks doubly linked list invariants before performing the unlink memory writes. If the invariants are violated, then a suitable abort() or panic() is called, depending on if user mode or kernel mode, preventing memory corruption from occurring. An example…

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: AI Experts Already Doomsday Prepping for When AI Takes Out the Entire Financial System: Start stocking up, folks!
items.content:
Powerful AI models are going on hacking sprees — or helping humans with them — left and right. If the AI industry doesn’t get its collective act together and stop its products from being used to such dangerous ends, it could be only a matter of time before one of these AI-powered hacks targets our essential infrastructure.

This is a scenario that some AI researchers are apparently already preparing for. Andreas Stuhlmüller, CEO and cofounder of the AI research company Elicit, recently rattled off a prepper-esque checklist of how to prepare for when AI-powered cyberattacks could take out financial systems, power grids, the internet, and all the other infrastructure that underpins modern life.

“Cash: Get a few weeks of spending in cash,” he recommended in a tweet . Then he suggests, in greater detail than we’ll get into here, getting a Starlink terminal in case your local internet network goes down; a battery, generator and solar panels for power; weeks worth of water and food; and a hand-crank emergency radio.

Stuhlmüller’s paranoid recommendations come after a shocking cyberattack that targeted the refrigerator systems used in hundreds of grocery stores across France. The as-yet unknown perpetrators cranked up the fridge temperatures up to 122 degrees Fahrenheit, spoiling food and even causing fires. The CEO of one chain targeted by the attack, Intermarche, said it caused losses amounting to “tens ​of millions of euros nationwide in a single day.”

AI’s role in the attack hasn’t been confirmed. But given AI’s ubiquity among coders, it’s likely that it was used to some degree. On top of churning out code, the tech is alarmingly good at identifying vulnerabilities . A recent CrowdStrike report found that there was a nearly 90 percent year over year increase in AI-enabled cyberattacks.

There’s also, of course, the recent disclosures from frontier AI labs like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta, over how their agentic AI systems broke out of their testing environments and launched cyberattacks against other companies’ websites and computer systems.

These incidents represent an alarming escalation in the threat AI poses to cybersecurity systems, not only assisting hacks but carrying themselves autonomously while also avoiding the detection of their human overseers.

All that being said, it’s a major leap to say that AI models — or humans using them — will go from hacking websites and supermarket fridges to your local power grid and banking system. But we can hardly blame anyone for being worried about this possible eventuality. Better safe than sorry, right?

items.title: How the Claude Code team does code review
items.content:
How do you review code at the volume agents produce it? On the Claude Code team, once we had high coverage and deep reviews, we started optimizing for the minimum amount of human review time that doesn't raise reverts or incidents.

We've said before that Claude writes about 90 percent of Claude Code's own code. So how do we review code at the volume we produce it? Does anyone read code anymore? And if something breaks, who catches it?

This post covers the code review flow on the Claude Code team and how it has evolved. From June to September, merged pull requests to Claude Code's codebase more than doubled while the share that had to be reverted fell by more than 40 percent.

We didn't remove review. But we did move most of the reading to machines, optimized for human time and attention, and invested heavily in making it fast and easy to undo mistakes.

When agents write code, the number of changes goes up, fast. In Anthropic's monorepo, changes landing per day went from about 2,500 in May to more than 30,000 in September this year.

Claude Code lives in its own repository, separate from the monorepo, but it's seeing a lot of pressure too. When you are shipping this fast, manual, line-by-line code review is incredibly difficult if not impossible.

This article mainly focuses on finding and fixing issues, but we will come back to the second job near the end.

We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?"

Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague.

Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny.

We want to preserve human time and attention for issues only humans can solve and make sure automated checks catch the rest. At our current rate of change, there is still an incredible amount of work for humans to do, and our team encounters new and novel challenges almost daily.

Human time covers both sides of review's cost: the time people spend reviewing, and the time they spend fixing what bad code breaks. Cutting the first doesn't help if the time just shows up in the second.

So the goal is that most pull requests in the Claude Code repos (the CLI, the desktop and web apps, and the mobile apps) merge with at most one human in the loop, who can be the author, with no increase in reverts or incidents. To measure human time, we track human approvals per PR (median and 95th percentile), human comments, and how long a PR waits on a person. Revert and incident rates are the guardrail: if they rise, we haven't saved human time, we've only moved it.

A typical change, from an engineer's laptop (or a Claude session in Slack), goes through multiple layers of code review.

Most review now happens before a PR exists. We give Claude something it can run—like tests, a build or a screenshot to compare against the design—and ask it to show the output instead of saying it's done. Then a subagent reviews the diff with fresh context. Both habits come from our best-practices guide .

Before opening a PR, many of us also run a few internal skills: one hunts for bugs, one simplifies the diff, and one checks the behavior end to end. UI changes also get checked against our design guidelines.

Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, has called giving Claude a way to verify its work probably the most important thing for getting good results. He estimates it makes the final result two to three times better, and writes, "Verification looks different for each domain. It might be as simple as running a bash command, or running a test suite, or testing the app in a browser or phone simulator."

items.title: JPEG XL vs AVIF for web use-cases
items.summary: compsci, web
items.content:
JPEG XL has now landed in all major browsers, so I figured I'd take a closer look at what it's good/bad at compared to other formats.

I'll go into full detail, with examples and benchmarks, but for those of you who don't have the time, here are the headlines:

For lossy photos on the web, AVIF almost always produces smaller files than JPEG XL. At default effort settings, the best JPEG XL version is typically 15–25% larger than the equivalent AVIF. At maximum effort settings, the gap narrows a little, to typically 6–20%. There are outliers, where JPEG XL is close to, or even beats AVIF, so if you want the absolute best result for a particular image, it's worth trying both. See the F1 image for a typical example, and the weasel for an outlier.

The JPEG XL encoder matters a lot. jixel , a newer JPEG XL encoder, usually produces smaller files than libjxl , except when the image has detailed transparency. The people image is one example.

For screenshots and illustrations, AVIF is much better than JPEG XL. The equivalent JPEG XL is 30–90% larger at default effort settings, and 20–70% larger at maximum effort settings. Lossy AVIF handles these well - you don't need to use lossless formats unless you really need bit-exact results. See the screenshot and illustration examples.

For images with transparency, AVIF is much better than JPEG XL. The libjxl version is 31–44% larger at default effort settings, and 61–70% larger at maximum effort settings. jixel always encodes transparency losslessly, which makes its files 2–3x the size of AVIF's. See the data .

AVIF is generally faster to encode, and uses less memory, when you factor in file size. jixel is faster than AVIF and uses less memory, but its files are typically significantly larger, so AVIF is better on balance. See the F1 image for one example.

AVIF is faster to decode. JPEG XL typically takes 2–3x as long to decode at medium quality, but the gap narrows at very high qualities, where Chrome can sometimes decode JPEG XL faster. The people image is one example.

Higher effort settings are worth it for AVIF and jixel, but not libjxl. libjxl's higher efforts are much slower, use a lot more memory, and barely improve the result. Sometimes they produce larger files than the default effort. The screenshot is an example of this.

AVIF's 4:2:0 mode (half colour resolution) shouldn't be your default. It rarely reduces file size, and it makes higher qualities harder to reach. Although, it is quicker to encode and decode. Stick with 4:4:4 if you don't have time to check both. The F1 image is one example, and the screenshot is an exception.

Quality settings are reliable for all the encoders. With a single quality setting, the resulting quality varies a bit between images, but all the encoders vary in the same direction, and in ways that seem reasonable. See the data .

Progressive JPEG XL is basically free at high effort. jixel recently added support for early progressive previews, and at its slowest setting they cost little or nothing, but at its default setting the files are 12% bigger. Firefox and Chrome support progressive JPEG XL. Safari still renders the final image, but doesn't show progressive previews. However, is this type of progressive rendering a good user experience? See the examples and data .

AVIF supports progressive rendering! It's Chrome-only for now, but it's in progress for Firefox. It's more complex than progressive JPEG XL, but it gives you more control over what the preview looks like, the files are usually smaller, and they're much faster to decode. See for yourself .

For HDR, JPEG XL lacks gain maps, which is a significant limitation compared to AVIF. The JPEG XL format supports gain maps, but they aren't supported by browser decoders, and the encoding story is messy/experimental. When comparing non-gain mapped HDR content, the two quality metrics I used disagree a lot, but they agree that JPEG XL produces smaller files compared to AVIF. See the examples…

items.title: The Opportunity for Heat Pumps to Put Downward Pressure on Electricity Rates
items.content:
A state-by-state assessment of how many homes could install heat pumps within today’s electric grid, how they will benefit electric rates and emissions, and recommended policies.

Residential energy affordability is an increasing concern as energy prices continue to rise. As electricity demand continues to grow, particular attention has focused on whether additional load growth will further increase electricity rates. Historically, however, the United States has shown that load growth does not necessarily increase rates. Between 1980 and 2000, electricity demand grew by more than 70% while inflation-adjusted retail electricity rates fell by approximately 26% , due in part to grid utilization improving by roughly 18% .

This report identifies residential heat pumps as an overlooked opportunity to further improve grid utilization by strategically adding additional electricity sales within available winter headroom — the available winter generation capacity after reserves above winter peak demand. In doing so, heat pumps can simultaneously put downward pressure on electric rates (i.e., lower rates relative to what they otherwise would be) and reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

Using seasonal generation capacity from EIA derated to meeting seasonal peak demand, and hourly load modeling from Evolved Energy Research (EER) and National Lab of the Rockies (NLR) normalized to real-world demand data, we evaluated:

Seasonal grid headroom varies substantially across states. Grid headroom can differ substantially between summer and winter. Most states in the Southwest, Upper Midwest, and Northeast have significant winter headroom (with peak demand in the summer), resulting in unused winter grid capacity. In contrast, many states in the Southeast and Pacific Northwest have similar summer and winter headroom, in part because of widespread electric resistance heating.

Roughly 109 million US homes — three out of four — could heat and cool with heat pumps within available winter headroom. This means an additional 86 million homes could install a heat pump, adding to the 23 million homes today. The appropriate deployment strategy varies by state based on existing seasonal capacity and demand:

These estimates reflect the capacity available under today’s grid and should not be interpreted as a limit on longer-term heat pump deployment as the grid evolves.

Strategic heat pump deployment can improve grid utilization and put meaningful downward pressure on residential electricity rates. In summer-peaking states, filling available winter headroom increases electricity sales without requiring new generation capacity, improving grid utilization and lowering the average cost of providing electric service. Given the caveats explored further in the report, these results should be interpreted as directional estimates that identify where the greatest opportunities exist rather than precise forecasts for individual utilities.

Heat pumps can substantially reduce greenhouse gas emissions when deployed within winter headroom. These results demonstrate that strategically combining all-electric and hybrid heat pumps can maximize emissions reductions within winter headroom while putting maximum downward pressure on residential electric rates.

Future changes to the grid, home energy efficiency, and weather will influence the headroom available for heat pumps. items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.summary_ko: YellowKey라는 제로데이 익스플로잇이 물리적 접근으로 Windows 11의 BitLocker를 우회해 암호화된 드라이브에 접근 가능하게 한다. 수 초 내에 보호를 무효화할 수 있다.
items.content_ko: 보안 연구자 Nightmare-Eclipse가 공개한 YellowKey 제로데이 취약점은 물리적 접근만으로 Windows 11 기본 BitLocker 보호를 우회할 수 있다. BitLocker는 Microsoft가 제공하는 전체 볼륨 암호화 기술로, 신뢰할 수 있는 플랫폼 모듈(TPM)에 저장된 복호화 키 없이는 디스크 접근이 불가능하도록 설계되었다. 많은 조직과 정부 계약업체에서 필수 보호 기술로 사용 중이다. YellowKey 익스플로잇의 핵심은 커스텀으로 만들어진 FsTx 폴더 사용으로, fstx.dll과 관련된 디렉터리는 Microsoft의 transactional NTFS 기술을 활용한다.

items.title: Withings now charges $100 per year to sync your data to other apps(including Apple Health and Google Health Connect)
items.content:
From 13 October 2026, Withings required accounts created from that date to have a Withings+ subscription to synchronize measurements with third-party applications, including Apple Health and Google Health Connect. [ 1 ] Accounts created on or before 12 October retained free synchronization, including when their owners purchased new devices. [ 2 ] The change added a recurring charge for affected users who wanted to send measurements from purchased hardware to other health apps; basic data and trends remained available in the Withings app without subscribing. [ 3 ]

Withings announced Health+ on 1 September 2022 as a service adding health analysis and habit-building tools to its Health Mate app. It was initially offered with the Body Comp scale and 12 months of access, with availability announced for 4 October 2022. [ 4 ] The company identifies Health+ as the former name of Withings+. [ 5 ]

Withings documents an Apple Health integration for sharing measurements such as weight, blood pressure and heart rate between applications. [ 1 ] Its US health-spending-account store page advertises Apple Health compatibility for its scales and watches. [ 6 ]

Withings' Apple Health support page dates the new-account requirement to 13 October 2026, attributing it to changes to its application programming interface (API) and privacy measures. [ 1 ] Its AI Connector frequently asked questions page links those changes to the introduction of its connector for artificial intelligence services. [ 7 ]

The developer Partner Hub separately dates its change to the Start for Free API plan to 12 October 2026. It states that accounts created after that date need membership to share data with free-plan applications, including existing integrations, and that Enterprise arrangements can lift the requirement for particular uses. [ 8 ] The consumer-facing support page identifies 13 October as the first affected account-creation date. [ 1 ]

As checked on 16 October 2026, the Withings website listed US prices of $9.95 monthly or $99.50 annually, and euro prices of €9.95 monthly or €99.50 annually. It offered a free month when adding the subscription to a device purchase. [ 3 ] The US App Store listing instead showed in-app offers of $9.99 monthly and $99.99 annually. [ 9 ]

For affected accounts, synchronization with third-party health applications became dependent on an ongoing subscription, although basic measurements and trends remained free in Withings' own app. [ 3 ] Engadget reported criticism from existing users over charging new customers for synchronization, while Numerama reported that Apple Health compatibility had influenced a buyer's purchase decision. [ 10 ] [ 11 ]

Apple describes HealthKit as an on-device repository through which applications can read and write health data with permission. [ 12 ] In a January 2025 support reply about Body Smart, Withings said its app required an internet connection for measurements to appear and synchronize with Apple Health. [ 13 ]

Matteo A opened the original Withings community discussion on 13 October 2026. Participants described plans to stop buying or recommending Withings products, or to postpone purchases. [ 14 ]

On Reddit's r/withings community, Mars0813 posted a screenshot of a subscription prompt encountered while setting up Apple Health sharing. The author said Apple Health compatibility had been the reason for buying the scale. [ 15 ] Another post, by teobiondo91, directed users to the official support discussion to request a reversal. [ 16 ] Comments in the setup thread included a statement by xxSeahawks that they intended to return a recently purchased BodyFit scale. [ 15 ]

On 15 October 2026 at 10:04, an official reply by “Markus From Withings” in the original discussion confirmed that accounts created through 12 October would retain free third-party synchronization. The exemption follows the account and continues when an existing user buys another Withings device. [ 14 ]

온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-110754 📢 Source: CPANSec 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False Text::CSV_XS versions before 1.65 for Perl leak the parsed fields of a record that fails to parse in getline. getline collects the fields of a record into a new array and returns a reference to it only when the parse succeeds. When the record has a syntax error, getline returns undef and never frees the array or the fields parsed before the error. A long-running process parsing untrusted CSV retains every malformed record it is sent, so repeated malformed input exhausts its memory. 📅 Published Date: 2026-10-16T22:06:46.839Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-110754
